This question is synced with an identical question on Metaculus. The original question opened on 2025-07-17 23:28:09 and can be found [here](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/38769). This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

[IMF Portwatch](https://portwatch.imf.org/), in partnership with the University of Oxford in the UK, offers satellite-based data on vessels to help users assess the impact of extreme events on global trade. Among the chokepoints it [monitors](https://portwatch.imf.org/pages/port-monitor) is the Strait of Hormuz, which is the only maritime passage from the Persian Gulf into the ocean. 

The Strait of Hormuz has long been the world's most important chokepoint for oil transit, from oil-rich Gulf states to the world's consumers of oil:

![](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/images/2012.01.04/Hormuz.png)(Source: the [US Energy Information Administration](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=4430))

Roughly 20% of the world's crude oil passes through the Strait each day. If shipping got cut off, it could have significant impact on the world's oil volumes and put sharp upward pressure on world energy prices. ([EIA](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=65504))  

Amid the [Iran–Israel war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Israel_war), there were reports in June 2025 that Iran was considering closing the Strait, with a Persian-language media source headlined "If America goes to war with Iran, closing the Strait of Hormuz is our legitimate right." **The Mystery of Iran’s Shadow Fleet: A Fleeting Light in the Gulf**

Analysts proposed three possible explanations: a defensive move to avoid legal justification for vessel seizures by demonstrating compliance with international maritime rules; a response to growing Chinese pressure requiring transparency for insurance and port access, as China accounts for over 80% of Iran’s oil exports; and an economic calculation to reduce logistical costs and increase revenue by avoiding the high expenses of the shadow fleet, including $100,000 daily VLCC rental fees, smuggling commissions, and losses from extended transit times. Despite the brief visibility, the fleet reverted to complete digital silence by October 17, 2025, leaving behind unresolved questions. Data from Kpler and TankerTrackers indicate Iran’s oil exports reached 1.95 million barrels per day in September 2025—its highest level since 2017—while production rose to 3.45 million barrels per day, surpassing Libya and Nigeria combined. Any significant disruption to shipping through the strait would have had devastating consequences for global trade and the economy. The strait is the only maritime route connecting the oil-rich Persian Gulf to the world ocean, carrying huge volumes of crude oil and liquefied natural gas from countries such as Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE, and Iran. Daily, around 20-21 million barrels of oil pass through the strait, accounting for approximately 20-25% of global oil consumption. Also, around 20% of the world's liquefied natural gas exports pass through the strait, with most of it coming from Qatar. Most of the energy resources passing through the strait are destined for Asian markets. In 2024, 84% of crude oil and 83% of liquefied natural gas passing through the strait were intended for Asian countries, including China, India, Japan, and South Korea. 'The blockage of the strait would have led to a sharp rise in global oil prices,' said a US official. Instead, global oil prices fell by more than 10% after US attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities, partly due to relief that the conflict did not cause significant disruptions to oil trade. US officials did not reveal how they detected the mines on Iranian ships, but such intelligence is usually gathered through satellite imagery, secret agents, or a combination of both methods.
